Fetal Echo Project · Unit D4 · Detect tier · v0.1

The four-chamber view in depth

DRAFT - NOT FOR CLINICAL USE. Contains claims with status 'ai-extracted' that no clinician has verified.

You will be able to

  • Judge heart size, position and axis.
  • Apply the criteria for the atria, pulmonary veins, ventricles, septum and atrioventricular valves.
  • Avoid the common false alarms: a pericardial rim and septal drop-out.
  • Say what a normal four-chamber view does not exclude.

More than a count

The four-chamber view requires much more than counting four chambers.1

Work through it in the same order every time: size, position and axis, then atria, veins, ventricles, septum, valves.

Size and the rim of fluid

A normal heart is usually no larger than one third of the area of the chest.2

A small amount of pericardial fluid, 2 mm or less in thickness at end-systole, is common in the second and third trimesters and is normal. A thin dark rim around the heart should not be mistaken for an effusion.3

Position and axis

The heart lies mainly in the left chest. Its long axis normally points to the left at about 45 degrees, plus or minus 20 degrees, relative to the front-to-back axis of the chest.4

An abnormal axis raises the risk of a cardiac malformation, especially of the outflow tracts, and may be associated with a chromosomal anomaly.5

A heart displaced from its normal position may point to a diaphragmatic hernia, a space-occupying lesion in the chest, or a small or absent lung.6

Atria

The two atria normally look similar in size. The flap of the foramen ovale moves within the left atrium. The septum primum, the lower rim of the atrial septum, should be present.7

The crux of the heart is the point where the lower atrial septum meets the upper ventricular septum and where the atrioventricular valves insert.8

Pulmonary veins

Where technically feasible, at least one pulmonary vein should be seen entering the left atrium on grey-scale. Colour can help but is not mandatory for this.9

If colour is used to show the veins, display it alongside the grey-scale image to help avoid false-negative findings.10

Ventricles

The moderator band near the apex identifies the morphological right ventricle. The left ventricular apex looks smooth and forms the apex of the heart.11

The ventricles should look similar in size, with no thickening of the walls.12

Mild disproportion can be a normal variant in the third trimester. Right-left asymmetry in mid-gestation is different: it warrants further examination. Important causes are coarctation of the aorta, an evolving hypoplastic left heart and anomalous pulmonary venous return.12

Ventricular septum

Examine the septum from apex to crux and, if possible, sweep from its most posterior part towards the outflow tracts.13

The septum is seen best with the beam perpendicular to it. With the beam parallel to the septum, acoustic drop-out can falsely suggest a defect near the crux.14

Small septal defects of 1 to 2 mm can be very difficult to confirm, particularly when fetal size or position is unfavourable. Most are of limited clinical significance and may close on their own before birth.15,16

Atrioventricular valves

There should be two separate atrioventricular valves that open separately and freely. The septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve inserts closer to the apex than the mitral valve: the normal offset.17

Abnormal alignment of the two valves can be a key finding in anomalies such as atrioventricular septal defect.17

Rate and rhythm

Normal rate is 120 to 160 beats per minute, with a regular rhythm.18

Unit D8 covers rate and rhythm in full.

What a normal four-chamber view does not exclude

Some lesions, for example transposition of the great arteries and coarctation of the aorta, may not be evident in the four-chamber plane alone.19

Complete transposition, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk and pulmonary atresia with a ventricular septal defect can have a four-chamber view that looks normal.20

What the fetal echocardiogram adds

These points are from the echocardiography guideline. They describe the specialist examination, not the screen.

The four-chamber view should be examined in at least two perpendicular planes, because the angle at which the beam meets a structure changes how it is seen.21

The cardiac axis must be assessed; measuring the angle is optional. A complete study requires a measured ratio of cardiac to thoracic area.22,23

Pulmonary venous connections must be shown from at least one vein on each side, with two-dimensional and colour imaging.24

Both two-dimensional and colour images are required to assess the ventricular septum and to locate any defect.25

Four-chamber view checklist

  • Heart usually no larger than a third of the chest area2
  • Mainly in the left chest; axis about 45 degrees to the left (plus or minus 20)4
  • Rate 120 to 160 per minute, regular18
  • Atria similar in size; foramen ovale flap moving in the left atrium; septum primum present7
  • At least one pulmonary vein entering the left atrium, where technically feasible9
  • Ventricles similar in size; walls not thick; moderator band near the apex of the right ventricle11,12
  • Septum examined from apex to crux, beam perpendicular where possible13,14
  • Two atrioventricular valves opening separately and freely; normal offset17
  • Pericardial fluid no more than a thin rim (2 mm or less)3
